headline_en: Bangladeshi expatriates: why narrow views develop despite living in liberal societies
summary_en: Opinion column by North South University teacher Mohammad Jalal Uddin Shikder, prompted by a 23 July 2026 incident in which a UK-based Bangladeshi spread a Fenchuganj head teacher's Facebook reel with a negative caption. He asks why some Bangladeshis long settled in Europe or America try to police social behaviour at home, cites diaspora research, and argues that Bangladeshi migration research focuses on labour markets and remittances and neglects identity. He notes that expatriates are now also connected to Bangladesh as voters.

facts.statement: On 23 July 2026, Beauty Rani Pal, head teacher of Pitaitikar Government Primary School in Fenchuganj, Sylhet, posted a Facebook reel; she alleged that a Bangladeshi living in the United Kingdom spread it with a negative caption, triggering wide social-media controversy, after which teachers and others across Bangladesh posted reels with the same song in solidarity (Prothom Alo, 26 July 2026).
facts.source_in_article: Column author citing Prothom Alo report of 26 July 2026

facts.statement: The columnist (Mohammad Jalal Uddin Shikder, North South University) says that Bangladeshis in Europe or America rely on host-country institutions such as state schools, health care, university access, low-interest education and home loans, pensions and other social security, while many maintain their own mosques, cultural organisations, community centres and mother-tongue schools.

The columnist says most migration research in Bangladesh focuses on the labour market and remittances, and very little studies how long residence abroad changes identity and views of the home country; he calls for more research on expatriate identity crisis, the new generation, social media and global events.
The columnist notes that Bangladeshi expatriates now contribute not only to the economy but are also connected to Bangladesh as voters.

summary_en: Prothom Alo investigation into political killings and extortion in Raozan, Chattogram: at least 26 murders from 5 August 2024 to June 2026, mostly tied to rival BNP factions, sand-quarry and construction-material control. Among the victims was a returnee from abroad, Manik Abdullah, shot at home on 19 April 2025. Expatriates building houses face extortion: one Noapara expatriate was asked for 25 lakh taka and went back abroad; a BNP notice alleged an Oman-based businessman was asked for 1.5 crore taka and his house burned.

facts.statement: Manik Abdullah, a Jubo Dal activist who had returned from abroad (probashferot), was shot dead at night in his own home at Bhandari Colony, Garibullah Para, Raozan, Chattogram, on 19 April 2025; his family has since left the house. Law enforcers and many locals believe followers of Jubo Dal leader Arafat Mamun were involved; Mamun's associate denies it.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo reporters, locals, law enforcement

facts.statement: In parts of Raozan (Kadalpur and nearby areas), house builders must hire masons and buy bricks, sand and cement from designated people tied to armed groups; bringing outside workers or materials is obstructed, so owners pay above market rates.

Armed men demanded 25 lakh taka from an expatriate in Noapara, Raozan, while he was building a house; he stopped construction and went back abroad, and relatives say he is not returning home for fear for his safety.

A BNP show-cause notice of 5 November 2024 accused local MP Giasuddin Quader Chowdhury of, among other things, demanding 1.5 crore taka from Oman-based expatriate businessman Yasin and burning his house; Giasuddin Quader denies all the allegations.
facts.source_in_article: BNP show-cause notice; Giasuddin Quader Chowdhury's denial to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Prothom Alo counted at least 26 killings in Raozan from 5 August 2024 to June 2026, with over 350 people injured in more than a hundred shootings and clashes; at least 16 killings were linked to political disputes, and six occurred after the BNP government took office in February 2026.

Chattogram district police say associates of Sajjad Ali Khan, a criminal hiding abroad, including Md. Raihan, Mobarak Hossain alias Emon, Md. Kader and Dhama Ilias, are extorting and working as hired killers in Raozan; Superintendent of Police Md. Masud Alam says drones are being used to locate them and checkpoints and patrols have been increased.

Jubo Dal leader Muhammad Jane Alam, who had returned to the Raozan area after 17 years and become active, was shot dead near Olimiar Hat on 5 January 2026; locals also mention a case against him over shooting at an expatriate's house and extortion.

headline_en: 'Sent two sons abroad hoping for happiness; had they stayed home they would be alive'
summary_en: Of 16 Bangladeshis killed in a fire at a sofa factory in Manfuha, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 13 were from Naogaon (12 from Atrai upazila, one from Naogaon Sadar). Relatives say workers were asleep and the factory's main gate was locked from outside. Families describe migration costs of 5 and 7 lakh taka and debts. The Naogaon DC says the embassy's labour welfare wing is working on identification and repatriation of bodies, which may take some time.

facts.statement: 16 Bangladeshis died in a fire at a sofa-making factory in the Manfuha area of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 13 were from Naogaon district (12 from Atrai upazila, 1 from Naogaon Sadar). Families learned of the deaths on Sunday night (9 August 2026) and the Naogaon Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Saiful Islam confirmed the 13 deaths on the morning of 10 August 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Naogaon DC Mohammad Saiful Islam; relatives

facts.statement: An uncle of victim Hasibul Hasan said the workers were sleeping in the Riyadh sofa factory when the fire broke out and the factory's main gate was locked from outside, so they could not get out.
facts.source_in_article: Anwarul Islam, uncle of victim Hasibul Hasan

facts.statement: Guffar Pramanik of Gondogohali village, Atrai, Naogaon, said sending his elder son Mohan to Saudi Arabia cost 5 lakh taka (about seven years ago, by mortgaging family land) and sending his younger son Sumon (about two years ago) cost 7 lakh taka; both died in the Riyadh factory fire.
facts.source_in_article: Father Guffar Pramanik; uncle Samad Pramanik

facts.statement: Mohan Pramanik mortgaged family land to go to Saudi Arabia about seven years ago, redeemed the land with his earnings, and two years ago took his younger brother Sumon to Saudi Arabia to work in the same factory.

The Naogaon Deputy Commissioner said the labour welfare wing of the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia is working on identifying the dead and bringing the bodies home; government and local administration are trying to bring them quickly after due process, but it may take some days.

Moyen Sheikh of Ujanpoi village, Atrai, said he is deep in debt from sending his son Farid Sheikh (who went to Saudi Arabia about a year and a half earlier, the family's only earner, with a wife and two-year-old daughter) and does not know how he will repay or run the household.

headline_en: We want to make US-Bangla a full aviation group: Abdullah Al Mamun
summary_en: Interview with US-Bangla Airlines MD Abdullah Al Mamun on adding 21 aircraft. He plans more flights to Gulf destinations and new routes to Kuwait, Madinah, Dammam and Salalah, and to make Chattogram and Sylhet hubs because many Middle East passengers come from those regions. He says airport charges, travel tax, excise duty and airport charges in Bangladesh are higher than neighbours', which makes fares high.

facts.statement: US-Bangla MD Abdullah Al Mamun said the international air passenger market from Bangladesh is about 70,000 crore taka a year, of which Bangladeshi carriers (US-Bangla and Biman) hold 30% (14,000 crore taka) and foreign airlines 56,000 crore taka; US-Bangla aims for a 15% share by 2027.
facts.source_in_article: Abdullah Al Mamun, MD, US-Bangla Airlines

facts.statement: US-Bangla plans, after adding 21 aircraft, to increase flights to Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah (UAE), Jeddah and Riyadh (Saudi Arabia), Doha (Qatar), Muscat (Oman), Kuala Lumpur, Singapore and Maldives, and to start new flights to Kuwait, Madinah and Dammam (Saudi Arabia), Salalah (Oman), Johor Bahru and Penang (Malaysia), Brunei, South Korea and Japan, among others.
facts.source_in_article: Abdullah Al Mamun, MD, US-Bangla Airlines

facts.statement: US-Bangla's MD said a large share of passengers to Middle East destinations come from the Chattogram and Sylhet regions, so the airline wants to make those two airports hubs by next year with direct Middle East flights, basing 4 Boeing aircraft in Chattogram and 2 in Sylhet; currently three foreign airlines carry 70% of passengers from Chattogram alone.
facts.source_in_article: Abdullah Al Mamun, MD, US-Bangla Airlines

facts.statement: US-Bangla's MD said landing, parking and ground-handling charges at Bangladeshi airports are much higher than in neighbouring countries, and passengers' travel tax, excise duty and airport charges are excessive, which is why airfares in Bangladesh are high.
facts.source_in_article: Abdullah Al Mamun, MD, US-Bangla Airlines

facts.statement: US-Bangla's MD said air travel in Bangladesh is growing 8-10% a year, driven by people travelling abroad for tourism, treatment, education and work; Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport effectively depends on one runway.

headline_en: Two boats capsize off Myanmar; over 500 Rohingya feared dead: UN
summary_en: UNHCR and IOM said in a joint statement (Thursday 16 July 2026) that two boats carrying over 500 people, mostly Rohingya including some from refugee camps in Bangladesh, left Rakhine in late June and are feared lost. The agencies say the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal route to Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand is the world's deadliest sea route; about 300 Rohingya and Bangladeshi nationals have been reported dead or missing on it so far in 2026.

facts.statement: According to a joint UNHCR-IOM statement issued on 16 July 2026, two boats carrying over 500 passengers, mostly Rohingya including some who came from refugee camps in Bangladesh, left Myanmar's Rakhine State in late June 2026; contact with one boat carrying about 250 people was lost shortly after departure, and another with about 280 people is believed to have sunk near Myanmar's Ayeyarwady coast on 8 July. Deaths are not yet officially confirmed.

Rohingya seeking safety and livelihoods make dangerous sea journeys on small wooden boats hoping to reach Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand; UNHCR and IOM said these voyages were outside the regular season, so sea conditions were more hostile and risky.
According to the UN, about 900 Rohingya refugees died or went missing in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2025, making it the deadliest sea route in the world for refugees and migrants.
According to UNHCR and IOM, about 300 Rohingya refugees and Bangladeshi nationals were reported missing or dead in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2026 so far.
In November 2025 a boat carrying Rohingya capsized off Langkawi near the Thailand-Malaysia border; about 12 people were rescued alive.

Five-year ban for false information in Canadian visa applications: IRCC takes hard line
summary_en: Canada's immigration authority IRCC recently warned that false information or forged documents at any stage of a visa or immigration application count as misrepresentation under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Consequences include refusal, a ban of at least five years, a permanent fraud record, and for those in Canada, loss of status, removal and possible criminal charges. The applicant is responsible even if an agent or consultant filled in the form.

facts.statement: Under Canada's Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), any forgery or alteration in documents such as passports, visas or educational certificates counts as 'misrepresentation'; hiding important information or giving wrong information in an application is the same offence, according to a recent IRCC warning.
facts.source_in_article: IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada) warning

facts.statement: IRCC lists the documents most often forged as: passports and travel documents; visas; diplomas, degrees and trade or apprenticeship certificates; birth, marriage, divorce, annulment, separation and death certificates; and police clearance certificates.

IRCC stresses that even if an agent or consultant fills in or submits the application, the applicant bears responsibility for all information in it and cannot shift the blame for false information to a third party.

IRCC says anyone who tries to get a Canadian visa or permanent residence with false information or forged documents may face: immediate refusal of the application; a ban of at least five years from entering Canada or applying again; a permanent record of fraud; and, if already in Canada, cancellation of status and removal, plus possible criminal charges depending on seriousness.

Experts advise people hoping to migrate to Canada not to fall for inducements or follow dishonest agents' advice, and to make sure their own application is truthful; IRCC asks people to visit a Canadian government link (printed as https://bit.ly/3XKMqDC) for details.
Canadian government information link on misrepresentation as printed in the article: https://bit.ly/3XKMqDC.

headline_en: Asylum claims in Canada collapse: asylum via student, visit or work visas no longer as possible as before
summary_en: Asylum claims in Canada by temporary resident visa holders (visit or student visas) fell 84% in two years, from 10,095 in April 2024 to 1,580 in April 2026, according to IRCC data. The article attributes the fall to Bill C-12 (Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act), in force from 26 March 2026, tighter screening of temporary visa applications, and digital portals with strict deadlines. Mismatches between reasons given for the visa and the later asylum claim are treated strictly.

facts.statement: According to IRCC (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada) data, 10,095 temporary visa holders applied for asylum in Canada in April 2024, against 1,580 in April 2026, an 84% fall in two years.

The 'Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act' (Bill C-12) took effect in Canada on 26 March 2026, making asylum eligibility conditions much stricter; it is a major barrier for people who try to claim asylum long after entering Canada.

Canada now strictly screens asylum claims by people who entered on visit or student visas; any mismatch between the reasons shown when getting the visa and the information given in the later asylum application is treated strictly, so using a visit or student visa as an easy path to permanent residence through asylum has become very difficult.

Canada has introduced digital portals and strict deadlines for asylum processing, and the rate at which ineligible claims are quickly identified and rejected or declared abandoned has risen; temporary visa applications with unclear or suspicious purpose are being refused more often.
New laws proposed on 19 June 2026 are expected by many to further restrict Canada's asylum system.

Canadian immigration experts say the situation is a warning to those who wanted to use asylum merely as an 'easy route' to settle; the government aims to protect only those genuinely facing risk to life.

headline_en: Permission to send abroad visa and consular fees collected by local agents
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank issued a circular on Monday 22 June 2026 allowing visa and consular fees collected in local currency by foreign embassies or their local visa processing agents to be remitted abroad through authorised dealer banks. Conditions: fees must be collected at the embassy's set rate, banks must obtain an embassy-issued invoice with applicant-wise fee details, and all applicable taxes must be deducted before remitting.

facts.statement: By a Bangladesh Bank circular issued on 22 June 2026, local visa processing agents may collect visa fees locally (in taka) and, through authorised dealer banks, remit them abroad to the bank account designated by the relevant embassy, its overseas office or authority.

Bangladesh Bank's conditions for remitting locally collected visa fees: visa fees must be collected at the rate set by the relevant embassy; an invoice issued by the embassy or its authorised agency must be obtained, with an applicant-wise statement of fees collected attached; and all applicable taxes must be deducted before the fees are sent.
